title: Providers, connection strings and testing
summary: One model, many databases; connection strings from configuration; and fast, honest tests with SQLite in memory.

steps.title: Providers
body: The **provider** is the package that speaks one database. Your model and queries stay the same; registration changes:

"The same" has limits. Providers differ in SQL dialect (`LIMIT` against `TOP`/`OFFSET FETCH`), types (`decimal` is stored as text in SQLite and cannot be sorted there; SQL Server has `decimal(18,2)`), case sensitivity of string comparisons, and features (`rowversion` exists only in SQL Server). Migrations are **provider-specific**: generate them for the database you deploy to.
Connection strings do not belong in code. Put them in configuration (`appsettings.json`, environment variables, a secret store) and read them:

steps.prompt: Match each connection string to its provider.
steps.explain: Each provider has its own connection string format. `:memory:` is SQLite's special name for a database that lives only as long as its connection.

steps.prompt: Where should a production SQL Server password go?
options: In a secret store or environment variable read through configuration
As a constant in the DbContext
steps.explain: Configuration lets each environment supply its own connection string, and secrets stay out of source control. `GetConnectionString("Shop")` does not care where the value came from.

steps.title: Testing with SQLite in memory
body: Tests that touch the database should be **fast**, **isolated** (each test gets an empty database) and **honest** (real SQL, real constraints). SQLite in memory gives all three:
using var connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=:memory:");
connection.Open();                                       // the database lives while this is open
Then every context made from those `options` shares the same in-memory database, which vanishes when the connection closes.

Why keep the connection open yourself? With `UseSqlite("Data Source=:memory:")`, EF Core opens and closes the connection around each command, and **each new connection is a brand-new, empty database**.

EF Core also has an `InMemory` provider, but it is not relational: no SQL, no constraints, no transactions. Tests pass there that fail on a real database. Microsoft recommends against it for testing; prefer SQLite, or the real database in a container for the final word.

code: using var connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=:memory:");
using (var db = new ShopDb(options)) { db.Database.EnsureCreated(); db.Items.Add(new Item { Name = "pen" }); db.SaveChanges(); }
steps.explain: With a connection string, `EnsureCreated` creates the tables on one connection, which then closes and takes the database with it; the query opens a new, empty one. Holding one open connection keeps a single database alive for every context built on it.

items: SQLite in memory with one open connection per test
The real database engine in a container, created per test run
The EF Core InMemory provider, to test a unique index
One shared database file that every test writes to
Mocking `DbSet<T>` to return a fixed list
steps.explain: Tests should run the real translation and constraints and start from a known state. InMemory and mocks skip SQL entirely; a shared file leaks state between tests.

steps.prompt: In production the environment variable `ConnectionStrings__Shop` is set. What does `builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Shop")` return?
options: That variable's value: `__` maps to the `:` in `ConnectionStrings:Shop`
The value from appsettings.json, because files win over environment variables
null: environment variables are not configuration
steps.explain: ASP.NET Core layers configuration sources, and environment variables override `appsettings.json`. A double underscore stands for the section separator, so each environment can supply its own connection string without code changes.

steps.title: A test helper
prompt: Write a reusable test fixture for a `ShopDb` that takes `DbContextOptions<ShopDb>`:
public TestDatabase() { ... }          // open an in-memory SQLite connection, create the schema
public ShopDb NewContext() { ... }     // a fresh context on the same database
public void Dispose() { ... }          // close the connection: the database disappears
The tests use two `TestDatabase` instances and check they do not see each other's data, and that the unique index on `Item.Sku` (configured by the tests' `ShopDb`) is enforced.
starter: public ShopDb NewContext() => throw new NotImplementedException();
template: using (var dojoDb = dojoA.NewContext()) { dojoDb.Items.Add(new Item { Sku = "P-1" }); dojoDb.SaveChanges(); }
using (var dojoDb = dojoA.NewContext()) Dojo.Eq("a second context sees the saved item", 1, dojoDb.Items.Count());
using (var dojoDb = dojoB.NewContext()) Dojo.Eq("another TestDatabase is empty", 0, dojoDb.Items.Count());
Dojo.Throws<DbUpdateException>("the unique index is enforced", () => dojoDb.SaveChanges());
Dojo.Check("no database file was written", !Directory.GetFiles(".", "*.db").Any(), string.Join(", ", Directory.GetFiles(".", "*.db")));
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.Entity<Item>().HasIndex(i => i.Sku).IsUnique();
hints: Keep the open `SqliteConnection` in a field; build the options once with `UseSqlite(connection)`.
Create the schema in the constructor with a context from `NewContext()`.
